name: IoT & Embedded Security
description: Security of IoT devices, embedded systems, firmware, and smart-home ecosystems.

ccs.narrative:
IoT and embedded security at CCS has addressed device firmware, smart-home automation, and safety of physical-world cyber-physical systems. The 2018 class revealed systemic risks in smart-home ecosystems: On the Safety of IoT Device Physical Interaction Control (CCS 2018) showed that physical interaction chains between IoT devices create safety hazards, If This Then What?: Controlling Flows in IoT Apps (CCS 2018) exposed information-flow violations in trigger-action platforms, and HoMonit: Monitoring Smart Home Apps from Encrypted Traffic (CCS 2018) demonstrated that misbehaving apps leave detectable network patterns even under encryption. Scission (CCS 2018) brought CAN-bus intrusion detection to automotive ECUs.

In 2019-2020, the focus shifted to firmware analysis. Charting the Attack Surface of Trigger-Action IoT Platforms (CCS 2019) systematically enumerated automation-rule attack vectors, Automatic Fingerprinting of Vulnerable BLE IoT Devices (CCS 2019) identified IoT devices at risk through their companion apps, and Examining Mirai's Battle over the Internet of Things (CCS 2020) measured the Mirai botnet's ongoing competition for vulnerable devices.

Black-box firmware fuzzing matured significantly: Snipuzz: Black-box Fuzzing of IoT Firmware via Message Snippet Inference (CCS 2021) fuzzed firmware without source code or emulation by inferring message structure from device responses. HoneyPLC: A Next-Generation Honeypot for Industrial Control Systems (CCS 2020) extended honeynet techniques to ICS/SCADA, capturing attacks including malicious ladder logic.

ndss.narrative:
IoT and embedded security at NDSS started with the sobering observation that smart-device ecosystems lack even the most basic security primitives. Fear and Logging in the Internet of Things (NDSS 2018) documented the forensic vacuum in consumer IoT, while IoTFuzzer (NDSS 2018) provided the first practical fuzzing methodology for firmware with inaccessible source code. Together they framed the community's agenda: find vulnerabilities and build defenses for a device class that was never designed with security in mind.

The 2019–2021 period produced a wave of detection and policy-enforcement frameworks. IoTGuard (NDSS 2019) dynamically enforced security and safety policies; Packet-Level Signatures for Smart Home Devices (NDSS 2020) enabled traffic-based device fingerprinting; and IoTSafe (NDSS 2021) discovered real physical interactions among devices to prevent unsafe automation rule combinations. Measuring botnets (Hajime, NDSS 2019) and cryptojacking (NDSS 2022) showed that IoT networks are an active criminal infrastructure.

The 2023–2025 papers reveal a maturing field grappling with real-world deployment challenges. EM Eye (NDSS 2024) showed that electromagnetic leakage from display interfaces exposes video content; Paralyzing Drones via EMI Signal Injection (NDSS 2023) extended sensor attacks to aerial platforms; and Evaluating Machine Learning-Based IoT Device Identification Models for Robustness (NDSS 2025) asked whether identification models survive adversarial inputs—a necessary step before deploying them in production network-security products.

sp.narrative:
IoT and embedded security at IEEE S&P addresses the unique challenges of resource-constrained devices: lack of source code, heterogeneous firmware, physical sensor attack surfaces, and consumer privacy exposure. The 2018-2019 baseline established the scope: Understanding Linux Malware (S&P 2018) characterized the malware ecosystem targeting embedded Linux devices, and SoK: Security Evaluation of Home-Based IoT Deployments (S&P 2019) systematized what the field actually knew about smart home security.

The 2020 wave expanded to firmware analysis and privacy labeling. Karonte: Detecting Insecure Multi-binary Interactions in Embedded Firmware (S&P 2020) analyzed inter-process communication in firmware binaries without source code. OAT: Attesting Operation Integrity of Embedded Devices (S&P 2020) applied control-flow attestation to MCUs. Ask the Experts: What Should Be on an IoT Privacy and Security Label? (S&P 2020) directly informed the US FTC's work on IoT labeling policy. SoK: A Minimalist Approach to Formalizing Analog Sensor Security (S&P 2020) provided a formal vocabulary for reasoning about physical transduction attacks.

From 2021, papers addressed dynamic analysis of firmware and fuzzing IoT apps. DICE: Automatic Emulation of DMA Input Channels for Dynamic Firmware Analysis (S&P 2021) solved the DMA peripheral emulation problem that blocked dynamic analysis. Diane: Identifying Fuzzing Triggers in Apps to Generate Under-constrained Inputs for IoT Devices (S&P 2021) bridged smartphone apps to IoT device fuzzing.

By 2022-2024, the focus shifted to drone security (SoK: Security and Privacy in the Age of Commercial Drones, S&P 2021), satellite security (Space Odyssey, S&P 2023), and supply-chain threats in embedded hardware, reflecting the expanding perimeter of connected devices.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers here (all USENIX 2018) map out the IoT security problem from several angles at once. Some take an offensive, systems-level view: BlackIoT: IoT Botnet of High Wattage Devices Can Disrupt the Power Grid (2018) showed that a botnet of heaters and air conditioners could be used to destabilize the bulk power grid, turning consumer IoT into a critical-infrastructure threat. Others looked at the software and platform layer, like Sensitive Information Tracking in Commodity IoT (2018), which applied taint tracking to smart-home apps, and at human factors, with Rethinking Access Control and Authentication for the Home Internet of Things (2018) recognizing that homes are multi-user, multi-relationship environments that classic access control ignores. A third strand attacked the devices themselves, from voice assistants in Skill Squatting Attacks on Amazon Alexa (2018) to sensor spoofing in Injected and Delivered (2018), while ACES (2018) and Inception (2018) began hardening and testing bare-metal embedded firmware directly.

A clear breakthrough across 2019-2020 was firmware analysis at scale. Because IoT firmware is hard to run outside its hardware, researchers built emulation and "re-hosting" techniques so firmware could be fuzzed automatically: FIRM-AFL (2019) introduced high-throughput greybox fuzzing via augmented process emulation, HALucinator (2020) re-hosted firmware by emulating its hardware abstraction layer, and Jetset (2021) and Fuzzware (2022) pushed targeted rehosting and precise MMIO modeling further. In parallel, the physical-sensor attack line matured from spoofing into striking demonstrations like Light Commands (2020), which injected voice commands into microphones using lasers, and defenses like SAVIOR (2020), which protected autonomous vehicles with physical invariants. Verified and cryptographic foundations also appeared, including VRASED (2019) for remote attestation and JEDI (2019) for end-to-end IoT encryption.

Alongside the device and firmware work, a large measurement and ecosystem-security thread grew up. All Things Considered (2019) gave the first large-scale empirical look at IoT devices in real homes, Looking from the Mirror (2019) probed device security through companion mobile apps, and Shattered Chain of Trust (2020) exposed flaws in cross-cloud access delegation. Voice assistants kept attracting scrutiny in SkillExplorer (2020), and The Circle Of Life (2021) characterized the full IoT malware lifecycle in the wake of Mirai.

Where the area stands now (2021-2022 here) is more holistic and deployment-aware. Firmware fuzzing has become precise and practical (Fuzzware, 2022), and bug-finding has scaled across many devices by exploiting shared input patterns in Sharing More and Checking Less (2021). Defense has shifted toward whole-system semantics: HAWatcher (2021) does semantics-aware anomaly detection across automated smart-home apps rather than per-device checks. And the agenda has broadened to the user's physical environment and privacy, with Lumos (2022) helping people find hidden IoT snooping devices in unfamiliar rooms. The arc runs from "IoT is insecure and even dangerous" toward scalable firmware analysis, verified building blocks, and context-aware, user-centric defenses.

top4.narrative:
The earliest cluster of work in this list (all 2018) staked out the threat surface of consumer IoT and smart homes from several angles at once. Some papers attacked the physical-cyber boundary: "BlackIoT: IoT Botnet of High Wattage Devices Can Disrupt the Power Grid" (USENIX 2018) showed that compromised high-wattage appliances could manipulate the bulk power grid, while "Injected and Delivered: Fabricating Implicit Control over Actuation Systems by Spoofing Inertial Sensors" (USENIX 2018) and "Skill Squatting Attacks on Amazon Alexa" (USENIX 2018) probed sensor and voice-interface trust. In parallel, a software-analysis line emerged for finding bugs in resource-constrained devices, exemplified by "IoTFuzzer: Discovering Memory Corruptions in IoT Through App-based Fuzzing" (NDSS 2018) and "What You Corrupt Is Not What You Crash: Challenges in Fuzzing Embedded Devices" (NDSS 2018), which named the core obstacle—embedded hardware does not fuzz like a normal program. A third thread treated the smart home as an app platform that needs information-flow and policy enforcement: "Sensitive Information Tracking in Commodity IoT" (USENIX 2018), "If This Then What?: Controlling Flows in IoT Apps" (CCS 2018), and "Fear and Logging in the Internet of Things" (NDSS 2018, provenance logging) all built tooling to reason about IoT/IFTTT-style automation.

Around 2019-2020 the field consolidated and matured along each of these threads. On the systematization side, "SoK: Security Evaluation of Home-Based IoT Deployments" (S&P 2019) gave the community a shared framework for the whole home ecosystem. Policy enforcement moved from static analysis to runtime with "IoTGuard: Dynamic Enforcement of Security and Safety Policy in Commodity IoT" (NDSS 2019), and the trigger-action abstraction got a dedicated threat model in "Charting the Attack Surface of Trigger-Action IoT Platforms" (CCS 2019). The firmware-fuzzing problem saw a major scalability jump with "FIRM-AFL: High-Throughput Greybox Fuzzing of IoT Firmware via Augmented Process Emulation" (USENIX 2019), and the re-hosting/emulation bottleneck identified in 2018 was tackled head-on by "HALucinator: Firmware Re-hosting Through Abstraction Layer Emulation" (USENIX 2020). Defenders also moved toward trustworthy hardware roots, with "VRASED: A Verified Hardware/Software Co-Design for Remote Attestation" (USENIX 2019) and "TIMBER-V" (NDSS 2019) bringing formal guarantees and enclaves to tiny devices.

Two cross-cutting shifts stand out in this period. First, network-traffic analysis matured into a precise inference tool—"Packet-Level Signatures for Smart Home Devices" (NDSS 2020) and the earlier "HoMonit: Monitoring Smart Home Apps from Encrypted Traffic" (CCS 2018) showed both the privacy risk of, and the defensive value in, encrypted device traffic. Second, physical-channel attacks grew more striking, culminating in "Light Commands: Laser-Based Audio Injection Attacks on Voice-Controllable Systems" (USENIX 2020), which injected commands into voice assistants with a laser. Usability and policy questions also entered top venues via "Ask the Experts: What Should Be on an IoT Privacy and Security Label?" (S&P 2020) and multi-user studies like "Understanding and Improving Security and Privacy in Multi-User Smart Homes" (USENIX 2019).

By 2021-2022 the area reads as several well-defined, deepening subfields rather than a frontier land-grab. Firmware analysis kept refining fidelity and scale, from black-box approaches in "Snipuzz: Black-box Fuzzing of IoT Firmware via Message Snippet Inference" (CCS 2021) to precise hardware modeling in "Fuzzware: Using Precise MMIO Modeling for Effective Firmware Fuzzing" (USENIX 2022) and multi-binary analysis in "Karonte: Detecting Insecure Multi-binary Interactions in Embedded Firmware" (S&P 2020). Anomaly detection grew semantics-aware in "HAWatcher" (USENIX 2021), and large-scale empirical study of the threat itself matured in "The Circle Of Life: A Large-Scale Study of The IoT Malware Lifecycle" (USENIX 2021), building on earlier botnet measurement like "Measurement and Analysis of Hajime, a Peer-to-peer IoT Botnet" (NDSS 2019). The throughline across all years: the field moved from demonstrating that IoT is broken, to building reusable analysis infrastructure (emulation, fuzzing, attestation) and runtime/policy defenses that account for IoT's defining trait—software decisions with physical-world consequences.
